title: Making AI work for SMEs: from policy to practice

p: Malta already uses AI. In 2025, 46.5 per cent of people in Malta used generative AI tools, the third-highest share in the European Union. Businesses have been slower to follow, and that is where the opportunity lies: productivity, measured as output per hour worked, remains well below the EU average, and AI is one of the tools that can raise it. Support is already in place, from a national regulatory sandbox with priority access for SMEs to dedicated grants for AI projects, yet many businesses still do not know where to start.

The Malta Employers has consistently led the conversations that matter to Malta's business community, from demographics and skills to the changing nature of work. Artificial intelligence now runs through all of them. During SME Week 2026, Malta Employers asks how Malta's businesses move from using AI to making it work for them: productively, safely and within the rules that now apply.

This brief sets the context and brings together the latest European and national evidence and the views of the public and private organisations that joined our September focus group to solicit further feedback.

For most SMEs, AI does not start with a large investment or a data science team. It starts with the repetitive, time-consuming tasks that software can now handle or improve: answering customer queries, book-keeping and invoicing, scheduling, marketing content and demand forecasting. For every hour saved, the owner can spend an hour on customers, strategy and growth. Getting there requires a clear path: awareness, hands-on demonstrations, sector-specific pilots, accessible advice and plain guidance on cybersecurity, data protection and the EU AI Act.

Across Europe, adoption is accelerating. In 2025, 20.0 per cent of EU enterprises with ten or more employees used AI technologies, up from 13.5 per cent a year earlier (Eurostat, 2025a). The Commission's Apply AI Strategy, published in October 2025, aims to boost adoption, particularly among SMEs and has transformed the European Digital Innovation Hubs into Experience Centres for AI, giving businesses access to testing facilities and regulatory sandboxes (European Commission, 2025).

Malta starts from a strong position. Its generative AI use rate ranks behind only Denmark and Estonia and is well above the EU average of 32.7 per cent (Eurostat, 2025b). Business adoption lags. The Commission's 2026 Digital Decade report finds that Maltese SMEs still face challenges in digitalisation and in adopting AI and data analytics (European Commission, 2026b). People are comfortable with the tools; their businesses have yet to organise around them.

The case for AI is also a labour market case. In 2025, 83.6 per cent of people aged 20 to 64 in Malta were in work, against 76.1 per cent across the EU (Eurostat, 2026a), so businesses have little room to grow by hiring alone. Each person employed in Malta produced 92.4 per cent of the EU average output, yet each hour worked produced only 80.2 per cent (Eurostat, 2026b). We make up the difference by working longer hours. AI acts directly on what each hour produces.

The rules are taking shape. Obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models started applying from 2 August 2025, and since 2 August 2026 the Commission's AI Office can fine providers of those models. The AI Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, gives businesses more time: obligations for high-risk uses such as recruitment and credit scoring due applicable, from 2 December 2027 and for AI built into regulated products from 2 August 2028. It also extends some simplified requirements for SMEs to small mid-cap companies (European Commission, 2026a). Malta implemented the AI Act through Legal Notice 226 of 2025, making the MDIA the national market surveillance authority and requiring it to give SMEs priority access to its regulatory sandbox and to run tailored training (Government of Malta, 2025). The task now is to make sure businesses know it is there.

In September we brought together senior representatives from Malta Enterprise, Business 1st, Tech.mt, MDIA, Malta Business Registry, Family Business Office, General Workers' Union, the Office of the Prime Minister, Malta Development Bank, Identità, Xjenza Malta, APS Bank, National Statistics Office and the Malta Institute of Accountants, together with independent consultants. Thirteen organisations followed up with written contributions, as reported below:

Professor Alexiei Dingli opened the discussion with a challenge. Many SMEs already use some form of AI, he argued, but using AI is not the same as exploiting its potential. Familiarity with one tool such as ChatGPT, is easily mistaken for an understanding of what AI can offer a business: "There's much more than that. We're just using a fraction." He also warned of a quieter risk: businesses drifting from a genuine human in the loop to a "human rubber stamper" who accepts AI-generated work, including code, with a confidence it has not earned.

Kevin J Borg, Director General of Malta Employers, was clear that AI is no longer a technology of the future, because companies have already embedded it. Our position is that AI should upgrade jobs rather than replace them, as part of Malta's move towards a more productive, higher-value economy. He noted that even international employers have no consensus on how far or how fast AI will reshape economies. That uncertainty is a reason to engage now.

The public bodies around the table shared one message: start with the problem and keep human judgement in the loop. The Artificial Intelligence Governance Unit within the Office of the Prime Minister reminded us that AI is one tool among several, and that cleaner data, a simpler process or conventional automation is sometimes the better answer. Identità is introducing an AI chatbot and a system that flags incomplete residence permit applications earlier, while its staff handle final assessments. The National Statistics Office uses AI across administrative and technical work but names information security and confidential data as its main concern. The Malta Development Bank has adopted a Generative AI Usage Policy built on accountability, accuracy, human oversight and limits on sensitive data. Malta Enterprise and Business 1st made the same case for SMEs and government alike: AI should answer a genuine business need, with safeguards for accuracy, transparency, data protection and human oversight.

Some organisations shared what they have learned from using AI themselves. APS Bank has moved from proofs of concept to structured adoption, with internal assistants supporting proposition development, customer intelligence and document analysis. Its advice to SMEs is practical: start with a business challenge, choose manageable use cases, set governance from the outset and invest in AI literacy. The Family Business Office used AI to screen more than 49,000 companies on the Malta Business Registry for signs of family ownership, which allowed it to reach more than 12,000 businesses directly, many of which have since registered. The Malta Business Registry, on its part, is building the foundations that make AI usable: structured data, APIs and the Malta Business Wallet, which applies a once-only principle to due diligence.

On funding, Malta Development Bank guarantees up to 80 per cent of eligible loans, and its Go-To-Market programme with Xjenza Malta adds an interest-rate subsidy and collateral support for innovative SMEs. Xjenza Malta's Digital Innovation Programme, run with MDIA, offers awards of up to €200,000 plus a €25,000 sub-grant for technical consultations, with MDIA sandbox participation a condition of entry. The government has also raised the Digitalise your SME scheme from €5 million to €15 million. SMEs can receive grants of up to €128,400, plus up to €107,000 more for projects that include AI, paid one year after completion against reports on productivity gains and ethical AI use (Government of Malta, 2026). MDIA also offers sandboxing, compliance support, DiHubMT services and the AI4All literacy programme.

Skills came up repeatedly. Tech.mt has proposed a budget to strengthen AI literacy among SMEs. The National Skills Council argues that the question is which tasks change, rather than which jobs disappear and is building tools, including a planned Skills Intelligence Platform, to help SMEs assess what their people will need. The General Workers' Union supports accessible training and reskilling so that businesses can move from awareness to implementation.

The research and our stakeholders point in the same direction. Malta's businesses already use AI. A skills shortage, uneven governance and uncertainty about where to start hold them back. The MDIA's sandbox, Xjenza Malta's funding, the Digitalise your SME grants and the Malta Development Bank's guarantees are all available; the task is to connect businesses with them.

Closing that gap is the task for 24 November. We want the conference to move from analysis to commitments: clearer routes to the support that exists, practical training that reaches SME owners and their staff, and simple governance guidance that lets businesses use AI with confidence and raise what each hour of work produces. Professor Dingli's warning about the human rubber stamping reminds us that productivity and responsibility must advance together.
We encourage you to take part and to bring your proposals. Malta Employers' will draw on them in the position paper we will publish after the conference for submission to Government.
